title: The Franciscan crown
hook: a seven-decade rosary of Mary's joys

segments.voice: Yesterday, two answers to a question nobody can check: was Christ God's rescue, or God's plan from the start? Your line was christ first. Which picture did your mind lean toward? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

A young man has a habit. Every so often he picks wildflowers, weaves them into a little crown, and sets it on the head of a statue of Mary. Then he joins the Franciscans, and in the friary there's no time for flower-picking. The crowns stop. He's heartbroken, so much so, the story goes, that he thinks about leaving. Then, as he prays, Mary appears to him. Don't be sad, she tells him. Instead of flowers that wither, weave me a crown that won't: say your prayers in honor of seven joys of my life. That, tradition says, is how a new kind of rosary began. Today, the crown of seven joys.
screen: `A CROWN OF WILDFLOWERS.` → `NO MORE FLOWERS IN THE FRIARY.` → `A CROWN THAT WON'T WITHER.`

segments.voice: The Franciscan crown, sometimes called the Seraphic rosary, is prayed on beads like the ordinary rosary, but with seven decades instead of five. Each decade is an Our Father and ten Hail Marys, and each one holds a joy. The first is the Annunciation, when the angel Gabriel greets Mary, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." The second is the Visitation, Mary hurrying to her cousin Elizabeth and the child leaping in Elizabeth's womb. The third is the birth of Jesus. The fourth, the wise men coming to adore him. The fifth, finding the boy Jesus in the Temple after three days of searching. Those five come straight from the Gospel of Luke and the Gospel of Matthew. The last two come from the Church's tradition. The sixth is the risen Jesus appearing to his mother, a meeting the Gospels don't describe but tradition holds. The seventh is Mary's Assumption into heaven and her crowning as queen. There's something very Franciscan about the shape of it. The usual rosary's mysteries take in sorrows as well as joys and glories. This one stays with joy, all the way through. It isn't that Franciscans deny sorrow. Tradition says Francis bore the wounds of Christ in his own body. But the family that told of perfect joy at a locked gate also made a rosary out of nothing but gladness, and gave it to Mary as a crown. And joy, here, isn't a mood. It's a list of things that happened: a greeting, a visit, a birth, a homecoming, a reunion. Each bead is a reason.
screen: `SEVEN DECADES, SEVEN JOYS.` · `FIVE FROM THE GOSPELS.` · `TWO FROM THE CHURCH'S TRADITION.` · `A ROSARY THAT STAYS WITH JOY.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: seven joys. Settle, and breathe. If you pray the rosary, you can say seven Hail Marys, one for each of Mary's joys: the greeting, the visit, the birth, the wise men, the boy found, the risen son, the crown. If you don't, try the same shape another way. Count seven joys on your fingers, from your own life or someone else's. A phone call that came. A child born. A person found after you'd lost track of them. A reunion. One finger for each, slowly. Don't hurry to the end. Let each one be a bead. The bell holds the time.
The Franciscan crown. A seven-decade rosary, a garland of Hail Marys woven around seven joys of Mary. Today's word.
Your line: seven joys. Today, before bed, name seven good things that actually happened, small or large, and count them like beads. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Franciscans and other Catholics pray the Franciscan crown on a seven-decade rosary, meditating on the seven joys of Mary, one joy for each decade.

notes: Origin legend (a young man who crowned a statue of Mary with flowers, became a Franciscan novice, and was told by Mary to pray in honor of her seven joys) is presented as tradition; the date usually given (early 15th century) is omitted.
Order of the seven joys: Annunciation, Visitation, Nativity, Adoration of the Magi, Finding in the Temple, the risen Jesus appearing to Mary, the Assumption and Coronation. Confirm.
The extra Hail Marys traditionally added at the end of the crown are omitted under the claims rule.
'Three days of searching' is from Luke 2:46; Luke 2 is cited as a paraphrase source.
Latin 'septem gaudia' in the original note: confirm.

Editor pass: 'the usual rosary moves from joy into sorrow and on to glory' left out the luminous mysteries, so it now says the usual mysteries take in sorrows as well as joys and glories; 'the order that sang of perfect joy' corrected to 'told of', since day 1212's story is told, not sung.
